issues.legal_issue: A lease that does not specify its purpose does not, merely because it concerns a shop, establish that the premises were let exclusively for commercial use.
material_facts: The lease document did not state the purpose of the letting.
The premises were a small shop occupied by a tenant carrying on a modest trade.
The tenant also used part of the premises for basic residential needs, and the landlord’s predecessor knew of and accommodated that use.
The court considered the circumstances of small tradespeople who may need to work and live in the same rented space.
issues.conclusion: The lease did not establish an exclusively commercial purpose incompatible with residential use of part of the premises.
issues.legal_principle: In interpreting a lease, the intended purpose is inferred from the document and the circumstances in which it was made, including the social setting. Welfare legislation should be interpreted in a tenant-protective manner, with attention to the position of the weaker party; the court applied the approach associated with Moti Ram v. State of Madhya Pradesh, [1979] 1 SCR 335.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and lease_purpose_unspecified and small_trade_shop and tenant_used_premises_for_livelihood

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control legislation.
predicates.lease_purpose_unspecified: The lease document did not specify the purpose for which the premises were let.
predicates.small_trade_shop: The tenant occupied a small shop to carry on a modest trade.
predicates.tenant_used_premises_for_livelihood: The tenant used the premises as part of the means of supporting and maintaining a livelihood.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding concerns an unspecified lease of a small trade premises used for livelihood, the lease does not, on those facts alone, establish an exclusively commercial purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s incidental residential use of part of premises while continuing the small trade for which they were let does not constitute use for a different purpose where it is not a substantial change in the mode of enjoyment.
material_facts: The tenant continued to work as a cobbler in the shop while cooking and sleeping in its rear portion on working days.
The tenant went home on days when the shop was closed.
The tenant’s wife had become mentally ill, and he brought her to the premises while he worked and cared for her there.
The landlord’s predecessor knew of the residential use and had provided a sink to facilitate it.
The tenant did not stop the trade and convert the premises into a residence or a substantially different business.
issues.conclusion: The residential use was incidental to the continuing trade and did not amount to use for a different purpose under Section 13(2)(ii)(b) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949; the statutory ground for eviction was not made out.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(b) concerns use of a building for a purpose other than that for which it was leased. In this context, a different purpose requires a substantial change in the mode of enjoyment, not minor variation or incidental residential use alongside a continuing small trade. The provision, as welfare legislation intended to protect tenants from unreasonable eviction, is interpreted in its social setting and with a proportionate assessment of the use.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_kept_trading and tenant_used_part_for_incidental_residence and landlord_knew_of_residential_use and not tenant_substantially_changed_use

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction of a tenant under rent-control legislation on the basis of the tenant’s use of the premises.
predicates.tenant_kept_trading: The tenant continued the trade carried on in the premises.
predicates.tenant_used_part_for_incidental_residenc: The tenant used part of the premises for residential needs while continuing the trade.
predicates.landlord_knew_of_residential_use: The landlord or the landlord’s predecessor knew that the tenant used the premises residentially.
predicates.tenant_substantially_changed_use: The tenant stopped the original trade or otherwise substantially changed the premises’ mode of use.

issues.definition: When a tenant continues the trade and uses part of the premises for incidental residence known to the landlord, without substantially changing the use, that residential use is not treated as a different purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who has been evicted is entitled to restoration of possession after the eviction order is set aside, even if the landlord has inducted another tenant.
material_facts: The court allowed the tenant’s appeal and set aside the eviction order.
The tenant had already been evicted.
The landlord had inducted another tenant into the premises.
issues.conclusion: The court directed the trial court to restore the former tenant to possession under Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure, notwithstanding the induction of another tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for restitution following reversal or variation of a decree or order; the court directed restoration of possession despite the subsequent induction of another tenant.

rule.if: appeal_against_eviction_order and eviction_order_set_aside and tenant_already_evicted and another_tenant_inducted

predicates.appeal_against_eviction_order: The tenant brought an appeal challenging an order for eviction.
predicates.eviction_order_set_aside: The appellate court set aside the eviction order.
predicates.tenant_already_evicted: The tenant had been removed from possession before the appeal was decided.
predicates.another_tenant_inducted: The landlord placed another tenant in the premises after the former tenant was evicted.

issues.definition: When an appeal sets aside an eviction order after the tenant has been evicted, the former tenant is restored to possession even if another tenant has since been inducted.
